problem:
The matrix $P$ is given below. Let ${p}_{1}$, ${p}_{2}$, and ${p}_{3}$ be the respective columns of $P.$
Determine if $B=\text{{}{p}_{1},{p}_{2}\text{}}$ is a basis of $\text{Col}(P).$ 
If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}$, where ${p}_{3}={x}_{1}{p}_{1}+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}.$

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

activity_context.topic_title: Finding a Basis of the Column Space of a Matrix

examples.knowledge_point: Determining Whether a Given Set Is a Basis of the Column Space of a Matrix With Two Rows
examples.problem:
The matrix $A$ is given below. Let $\mathbf{a}_1$, $\mathbf{a}_2$, and $\mathbf{a}_3$ be the respective columns of $A.$ Determine if ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066433/assets/f7e27a29b580edc016bf479e983cb17c5e61ebb800b03e671b89b5d556056533.png) is a basis of $\textrm{Col}(A).$ 
If that is the case, find $x_1 \cdot x_2$, where $\mathbf{a}_3=x_1\mathbf{a}_1+x_2\mathbf{a}_2.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066433/assets/cce279327716181e5b5c5c1e95e7eac34c2b93a78a1f7e773393ffbf608cb1f4.png)
examples.worked_solution:
First, we reduce the matrix $A$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 9 \\ 3 & 1 & 17\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 9 \\ 0 & -5 & -10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=(-\frac{1}{5}){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 9 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So, a basis of $\textrm{Col}(A)$ is $\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2 \},$ that is to say,

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066433/assets/f083a27cf3de0a6150020b6f5887096258880d4f5e30de1cfb3bb091b79a16f9.png)

Now, since the $3$rd column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express $\mathbf{a}_3$ as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. So, we have

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066433/assets/96f39576ea8196a88248035262eb7cd006c134717f695b23c575667b6562f6e0.png)

This gives us $x_1 \cdot x_2 = 5 \cdot 2=10.$

feedback.problem:
Given the matrix 
$G=[\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ 2 & -\frac{8}{3}\end{aligned}].$ Find a basis $B$ of $\text{Col}(G).$
feedback.worked_solution:
In order to find a basis of $\text{Col}(G),$ we reduce the matrix $G$ to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned}G & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ 2 & -\frac{8}{3}\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{4}{3} \\ 2 & -\frac{8}{3}\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1}^{′} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{4}{3} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The pivot columns correspond to linearly independent vectors, while the non-pivot columns correspond to linearly dependent vectors that can be removed. Here, only the $1$st column is a pivot column, while the $2$nd column is a non-pivot column.

Remember that we need to pick the pivot columns from the *original matrix*, not from the reduced one. 

The $1$st column from the original matrix is ${g}_{1}.$ So, a basis of $\text{Col}(G)$ is ${{g}_{1}},$ that is to say, 

$$
B={[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}.
$$
